title: The Watchman and the News That the City Has Fallen
summary: God renews Ezekiel's appointment as a watchman who must warn the wicked, and answers the exiles' despair: he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked and calls them to turn and live. A fugitive arrives with the news that Jerusalem has fallen, and the prophet's mouth is opened. God then rebukes the survivors in Judah who claim the land while living in sin, and the exiles who enjoy Ezekiel's preaching like a love song but never obey it.
story: This chapter is the hinge of the book. For years Ezekiel had warned that Jerusalem would fall, while the exiles hoped it would stand. In chapter 24 God told him that on the day the siege began his wife would die and that he would be silent until a survivor brought news of the city's end. Chapters 25 to 32, the oracles against the nations, fill that interval. Now the fugitive arrives, the prophet's word is proved true, and his mouth is opened. The watchman commission, first given at his call (3:16-21), is repeated because his ministry is beginning again on new ground. From here on, the book turns from judgment toward restoration, though this chapter makes clear that restoration will not come to people who only listen.
historical:
The fugitive reaches Ezekiel on the fifth day of the tenth month of the twelfth year of the exile (verse 21), about January 585 BC on the most common reckoning. Babylon had breached Jerusalem's walls in the fourth month of Zedekiah's eleventh year, and the temple was burned about a month later (2 Kings 25:2-9; Jeremiah 52:5-13). If the city fell in the summer of 586 BC, the news took about five months to arrive, a reasonable time for the road from Judah to Babylonia (compare Ezra 7:9, where Ezra's trip took about four months). Scholars who date the fall to 587 BC either count Ezekiel's years differently or follow a few Hebrew manuscripts and ancient versions that read the eleventh year here.

Verses 24 to 29 look back to Judah. Babylon left the poorest people of the land behind to work the vineyards and fields (2 Kings 25:12), and after the assassination of the governor Gedaliah (2 Kings 25:25; Jeremiah 41), conditions there were chaotic. Some who remained apparently saw themselves as the rightful heirs of the land, the true Israel, while the exiles were cut off.
cultural:
Ancient cities posted watchmen on walls and towers. The watchman's job was to see danger early and sound the shofar, a ram's horn trumpet, so the people could take refuge or prepare to fight. His failure could cost the city, and a community rightly held him responsible. God uses that familiar office to define the prophet's duty.

The charges against those in the land in verse 25 draw on Israel's law. Eating meat with the blood in it broke one of the oldest food laws (Genesis 9:4; Leviticus 17:10-14), and shedding blood, idolatry, and adultery were the most serious violations of the covenant. The claim that Abraham was one man and they were many turned the patriarch's story into a title deed; God answers that the land was never a possession held apart from faithfulness. Verses 30 to 32 show another familiar scene: the prophet as local celebrity, discussed in doorways, attended like a performance by a skilled singer.
literary: The chapter is built from four units. Verses 1 to 9 are case teaching: a general case (a city's watchman) followed by its application to Ezekiel. Verses 10 to 20 restate the argument of chapter 18 in a disputation, a prophetic form in which the people's saying is quoted and then answered: they say their sins are too heavy to live under, and later that God's way is not just. The narrative of verses 21 to 22 is brief and stark, and it releases the tension built since chapter 24. Verses 23 to 33 contain two more disputations, one against the survivors in Judah and one against the exiles themselves. The chapter closes on the phrase that they will know that a prophet has been among them, a variation on the book's refrain.

outline.t: Turn and live: God's justice defended
The city has fallen, and the prophet's mouth is opened
Against those who claim the land in the ruins

doctrines.note: The call "Turn! Turn from your evil ways! For why should you die, O house of Israel?" (verse 11) is one of the clearest in Scripture. The past does not seal the future: the wicked who turn will live, and none of their sins will be held against them (verse 16).
God swears by his own life that he takes "no pleasure in the death of the wicked" (verse 11). Judgment is real, but it is not what God desires; his heart in judgment is to save.

God will "judge each of you according to his ways" (verse 20). Past righteousness is not a bank account against present rebellion, and presumption, whether based on ancestry or on religious attendance, offers no shelter.
The chapter ends by distinguishing hearing from doing. The exiles hear the word with pleasure but do not put it into practice (verses 31 to 32). God's word is meant to be obeyed, not admired.

words.note: Tsaphah, to watch, keep watch. The participle is the word for a watchman, a lookout posted to see danger coming. It defines the prophet as someone responsible for what he sees, not merely a commentator.

Shuv, to turn or return, and in this sense to repent. It is the Old Testament's main word for repentance, pictured as a change of direction on a road. It appears nine times here, and the call in verse 11 doubles it for urgency.
Zahar, to warn. Eight times in the chapter. The watchman's whole task is summed up in this word: he cannot make people turn, but he must make sure they have been warned.
Takan, to measure or weigh, here meaning to be right or just. The people say the Lord's way is not fair; God answers that it is their way that doesn't measure up.

christ: Jesus stands in the line of the watchmen who warned and called Israel to turn, and his first preaching was a call to repent because the kingdom of heaven had come near (Matthew 4:17). Ezekiel 33:11 lies behind the New Testament conviction that God is patient, not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance (2 Peter 3:9; compare 1 Timothy 2:4). Jesus also warned against the audience of verses 30 to 32: the one who hears his words and does not do them is like a man who builds his house on sand (Matthew 7:24-27), and James urges hearers to be doers of the word (James 1:22). The link is not a prediction but a shared pattern. And where Ezekiel could only warn, the gospel announces that Christ himself bore the sins that the exiles felt were too heavy to live under.

hard.q: Is God really fair if one sin can cancel a lifetime of righteousness, and one turn can cancel a lifetime of wickedness?
hard.a: The exiles raised this very objection (verses 17 and 20). The difficulty is real: the passage seems to judge a person by their last direction rather than by a total. Interpreters answer in a few ways. Many note that Ezekiel is not describing a single slip but a settled turn, a righteous person who trusts in his own record and then commits iniquity as a way of life (verse 13). Others stress that the passage is pastoral before it is systematic: it is spoken to people crushed by guilt (verse 10), to tell them the past does not have to decide their future, and to people who presumed on their past, to tell them it cannot protect them. Christian traditions differ on what this means for the perseverance of believers; Reformed readers usually take the warnings as a real means by which God keeps his people, while Wesleyan and Arminian readers take them as showing that a believer can truly fall away. On any reading, the passage's main claim is that God is not keeping a ledger to trap anyone; he is calling everyone to turn and live.

questions: The people said their sins were too heavy for them to live (verse 10). How does God's answer speak to someone who feels their past has disqualified them?
What is the difference between enjoying good preaching and obeying it? Where might you be like the audience in verses 30 to 32?
The survivors in Judah used Abraham's story to claim the land while ignoring God's commands. How can people use the promises of Scripture to excuse themselves?
